lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: Say It Like You Mean It
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 1, Session 2
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 1 Session 2
lesson.fileName: Session 2 - Say It Like You Mean It.pptx

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA08 vocabulary chosen for precise meaning (modal words); VC2E5LA05 complex sentences used for effect (a fronted because-clause); VC2E5LY10 creating persuasive texts for purpose and audience
plan.shape: ladder then upgrade: sort words by strength, upgrade weak claims, then front the reason, because a sure-sounding claim is the first thing a reader judges
plan.criticalFeature: the modal word sets how sure the writer sounds; louder is not stronger
decisionPoints: the High, medium or low? round
the choice check: which is the strongest position statement?
the exit board: a new weak claim upgraded
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today is still Claim it: say your side like you mean it.
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 1? Give the Issue Card Scaffold, have them choose question A, B or C, then join the upgrade round.

studentTools: Writing books with yesterday's Issue Card
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: A three-step ladder on the board: low (might, could), medium (should, probably), high (must, will)
Space to collect upgraded claims for the Issues Wall

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we make our side sound like we actually mean it.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for students who need a first step. Draw the modality ladder on the board before the session.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write a position statement that sounds sure and strong.
successCriteria: I can find the words that show how sure a writer is.
I can upgrade a weak opinion into a strong position statement.
I can start my statement with a because-clause for extra punch.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Yesterday you picked a side. Today you say it like you mean it.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Spotting the sure words is where we all start.
Upgrading a weak opinion is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 spotting modal words is reachable for all; SC2 upgrading a weak claim is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 the fronted because-clause is the stretch.

slides.title: Which one would convince the principal?
lines: Maybe we could perhaps have a slightly longer lunch?
Because tired kids can't learn, we must have a longer lunch.

notes.answer: the second - it sounds sure and gives the reason first
beats: SAY: Two students want a longer lunch. Same idea.
Only one of them will get a yes.
ASK: Which one would convince the principal? First or second?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, 1 or 2... show me.
EXPECT: 2
ASK: What makes the second one stronger? Name one word.
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: must; because; it sounds sure
SAY: Some of you may remember because-clauses from Term 3. Today they become a weapon.
trap: saying the first is better because it's polite.
Fix: ask which one sounds like the writer believes it. Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Launch reconnects Term 3 complex sentences (Week 7, main and subordinate clauses) to persuasion. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: How sure or how strong a word makes an idea sound.
slides.example: might (not sure) - should (fairly sure) - must (very sure)

notes.answer: how sure or how strong a word makes an idea sound
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Modality. Say it with me. Modality.
SAY: Modality is how sure a word makes you sound.
Like a thermometer: might is cool, must is boiling hot.
ASK: Which is hotter: We could act, or We must act?
5 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: must
trap: thinking more exclamation marks means higher modality.
Fix: cover the punctuation, ask which word is sure. Student points to the modal.
notes.prep: The one technical word today, used beside its plain meaning: how sure it sounds.

slides.title: Turn up the heat
lines: Weak: Maybe zoos could stop keeping polar bears.
Strong: Zoos must stop keeping polar bears.
Punch: Because polar bears roam huge distances, zoos must stop keeping them.

notes.answer: swap low words for high ones, then put the reason first with a comma
beats: POINT to Weak.
SAY: Maybe and could. I don't sound like I believe it.
I'll cross out maybe and swap could for must.
POINT to Strong.
SAY: Zoos must stop. Now I sound sure.
POINT to Punch.
SAY: Now the reason goes first: Because polar bears roam huge distances, comma.
The reader gets the why before the claim lands.
ASK: Where does my comma go in the punch sentence?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: after distances, at the end of the because part
trap: keeping maybe and adding must: Maybe zoos must...
Fix: student crosses out every low word first, then rereads.
notes.stretch: Use a high word that isn't must: will, need to.
notes.help: Point to the ladder and swap one word at a time.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: the modal word sets how sure you sound; louder is not stronger.

slides.title: Low, medium or high?
slides.pivot: find the modal word together, then place it on the ladder
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which word told you?

items.text: People might want to think about the Arctic.
We must protect polar bears now.
Governments should fund more Arctic research.
Perhaps tourists could stay further away.
Without a doubt, plastic is harming our oceans.
items.say: High. No must here, but without a doubt sounds certain. Tick or fix.

items.answer: 1 or 2 - loud, but it doesn't claim anything sure
items.say: Loud is not strong. There's no sure claim here. Tick or fix.

say: One finger low, two medium, three high.
Find the word that shows how sure the writer is.
trap: judging by capitals and exclamation marks.
Fix: cover the punctuation, student finds the modal word.
notes.stretch: Rewrite the low ones as high.
notes.help: Underline the modal word with a finger first.
notes.prep: Guided sort. Edge cases: a phrase (without a doubt) and a loud sentence with no modal. SC1.

slides.title: Which is the strongest position statement?

options.text: I think maybe zoos are not that great.
options.misconception: keeps the low words; vague about what should happen

options.text: Zoos must stop keeping polar bears.
Zoos are really, really, really bad!!!
options.misconception: mistakes loud for strong; no clear position

notes.answer: B - zoos must stop keeping polar bears
beats: SAY: Same topic, three writers. Who sounds sure and clear?
ASK: Which is the strongest position statement?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: what does C forget to say?
Less -> read each aloud calmly, ask which is sure, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. It says exactly what should happen, and must makes it sure.
trap: pointing to C because it sounds passionate.
Fix: ask what should happen, according to C? Student finds nothing.
notes.prep: First decision point, new sentences. Under 80% means a second ladder round before the upgrade round.

slides.title: Upgrade it
slides.pivot: cross out the low words together, then pick from the ladder
slides.followUp: cold call two boards: read yours like you mean it

items.text: Maybe kids could pick up a bit of rubbish.
items.answer: Every student must pick up rubbish they see.
items.expect: a must or will statement saying who does what

items.text: Perhaps people might use less plastic.
items.answer: We should stop using single-use plastic.
items.expect: should or must, and what exactly to stop

items.text: It could be good to save some energy.
items.answer: Families must switch off lights to save energy.

items.text: Scientists might possibly need more money.
items.answer: Governments must give Arctic scientists more funding.
items.expect: who must give what to whom

say: Upgrade each one so it sounds sure and says who must do what.
trap: changing the word but keeping it vague, like People must do stuff.
Fix: ask who must do what? Student names both.
notes.stretch: Add a because-clause at the front.
notes.help: Keep the sentence, swap only the low word for must.
notes.prep: Guided upgrading on new claims. SC2.

slides.title: Put the reason first
slides.pivot: say it aloud with a pause where the comma goes
slides.followUp: cold call one board: where is your comma and why?

items.text: We must cut pollution. Polar bears are losing their ice.
items.answer: Because polar bears are losing their ice, we must cut pollution.

items.text: Schools should plant more trees. Trees cool the playground.
items.answer: Because trees cool the playground, schools should plant more of them.
items.expect: Because trees cool the playground, schools should...

items.text: Everyone must recycle. Landfill is filling up fast.
items.answer: Because landfill is filling up fast, everyone must recycle.
items.expect: Because landfill is filling up fast, everyone must recycle.

say: Some of you may remember this from Term 3.
Join the two sentences: reason first, comma, then the claim.
trap: leaving out the comma after the because-part.
Fix: student reads it aloud, pauses, adds the comma at the pause.
notes.stretch: Try Since or Unless instead of Because.
notes.help: Write Because first, then copy the reason sentence after it.
notes.prep: Retrieval of Term 3 Week 7 subordinate clauses, now used for effect. SC3.

slides.title: Turn up the heat on your issue
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet: rate, upgrade, fix, then write your own strong opening.

beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Use yesterday's issue. Write it weak first, so you can feel the difference.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Check the punch sentence has a comma after the because-part.
TIME 15 minutes.
At 10 minutes, read two punch sentences aloud for the Issues Wall.
trap: a strong claim, then a paragraph full of maybe and might.
Fix: student circles every low word in the paragraph and upgrades it.
notes.stretch: Extension: modality for different readers, and a fair concession.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: a word sort, first answers done, the because frame.
notes.prep: Independent application on each student's own issue. The opening paragraph is reused when drafting in Week 4. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in three versions of the student's position and a strong opening paragraph

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Perhaps the canteen might sell a bit less junk food.
Upgrade it. Make it sure and put a reason first.

notes.answer: e.g. Because junk food makes us sluggish, the canteen must stop selling it
beats: SAY: A new weak claim. Show me you can turn up the heat.
ASK: Upgrade this claim, with the reason first.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Because..., the canteen must...
RECORD who keeps a low word or loses the comma. Tomorrow's warm-up group.
trap: Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 (upgrade) with SC3 (fronted reason) on a new topic. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read your punch sentence to your partner like a news reader. Did it sound sure?

notes.answer: open - listen for a high modal word and a reason first
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can upgrade a weak opinion?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Read your punch sentence to your partner like a news reader.
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: Because..., we must...
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. Tomorrow's warm-up group comes from both. SC2.

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: rate modality, upgrade weak claims, fix a comma, then write your own strong opening.
resources.title: Say It Like You Mean It
resources.subtitle: Strong words, sure claims, reasons first.

items.prompt: Find the modal word. Is it low, medium or high?

example.answer: Our school must recycle every bottle and can.

items.prompt: Rewrite each weak claim so it sounds sure.
rows: I guess bikes are sort of good.
Maybe the canteen could sell fruit.
Perhaps we might plant a garden.
answers: I guess bikes are sort of good.
Every family should ride bikes more often.
Maybe the canteen could sell fruit.
The canteen must sell fresh fruit every day.
Perhaps we might plant a garden.
Our school will plant a vegetable garden.

example.prompt: Join: We must save water. Dams are low.
steps: Add the reason, then a comma
example.answer: Because dams are low, we must save water.

items.prompt: Which sentence has the comma in the right place?
options: Because, bins are full we recycle.
Because bins are full, we recycle.
Because bins are full we, recycle.
items.explain: The comma goes at the end of the because-part, where you pause.

items.prompt: Lily joined two sentences. Find her mistake and fix it.
work: Polar bears are hungry because. We must act.
items.answer: The because-part is broken off. Fix: Because polar bears are hungry, we must act.

example.prompt: Issue: should zoos keep polar bears?
steps: Add 3-4 sentences to open your argument
example.answer: Because polar bears roam huge distances, zoos must stop keeping them.

items.prompt: Write your position three ways: weak, strong and punch. Then write a 4-5 sentence opening.
items.answer: Three versions, then an opening with a high modal word and a reason.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: choose modality to suit the reader, and use a fair concession.
resources.title: Modality Masters
resources.subtitle: The right strength for the right reader.

example.prompt: Claim: kids need more play time. Reader: the principal.
steps: Too strong sounds rude; too weak sounds unsure
example.answer: We strongly believe students should have more play time.

items.prompt: Write the claim for each reader. Choose your modal word carefully.
columns: Claim: we need a school garden
answers: We believe our school should build a garden.
We have to get a garden!
The council must fund school gardens now.

example.prompt: Zoos must stop keeping polar bears, although some zoos do help research.
steps: Medium modality for the other side
example.answer: Must for my claim; do help (medium) for the fair point.

items.prompt: Which writer sounds sure AND fair?
options: Zoos must close, and anyone who disagrees is wrong.
Zoos should change, although some do help research.
items.explain: The second: sure about the change, fair to the other side.

items.prompt: Sam mixed his modal words. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Zoos must maybe close their polar bear areas.
items.answer: Must and maybe fight each other. Fix: Zoos must close their polar bear areas.

items.prompt: Write a paragraph on your issue: high modality for your claim, medium for one fair point.
items.answer: A claim with must or will, a fair point with might or some, joined smoothly.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: a word sort, a first answer done and a sentence frame.
resources.title: Strong Words Helper
resources.subtitle: Use the ladder: might is low, must is high.

items.prompt: Sort the words: LOW or HIGH.
Swap the low word for must.
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.prompt: Bins are full. We must recycle.
steps: Add the reason and a comma
example.answer: Because bins are full, we must recycle.

items.prompt: Finish the frame for your issue: Because ___, we must ___.
items.answer: A because-part, a comma, then a must claim.
items.hint: Use your Issue Card from Session 1.

items.prompt: Write one more sentence that says why it matters.
